newsitem.title: USA: Away on Business: Hear this.
newsitem.headline: Away on Business: Hear this.

text.p: Frequent travelers who battle ear pain from cabin pressure changes appear to be picking up on a relatively new device designed to ease the problem.
It's a re-invented earplug called EarPlanes.

"Sales are running about six times the level they were last March. I can see a really great future," says Victor Kiam, the chief executive officer of Remington Products, who is the principal investor in Cirrus Products, maker of the plugs.
Kiam -- familiar to television viewers as the entrepreneuer who says he liked the shaver so much he bought the company -- has a similar story about the earplugs.
His wife had an ear drum problem and was reluctant to take a flight from Bermuda, he said. She used the plugs "and they worked perfectly."
The plastic plugs have a filter "which acts as an air lock and gradually allows air in," Kiam says. "This is the only non-invasive preventitive for ear pain, sinus problems, things like that."

He said about a third of the flying public has some sort of ear discomfort and about 5 percent to 6 percent of those "have very severe problems." In addition others have occasional trouble when they suffer from colds or sinus problems, Kiam said.
The new plugs are disposable, designed for one round trip. Because ear wax, dust or other particles entering the plugs could reduce their effectiveness they are not deisgned for repeat use, he said.

The plugs sell for under $5 a pair. There is also a version designed for children aged three to 11 and Kiam said the company will in January introduce a version of the product for infants, who are especially sensitive to pressure changes.
Also in early 1997, Kiam said, the products will be launched in Britain and Australia.
Kiam's interest in travel products goes beyond the plugs. In 1990 he bought Franzus Co. Inc., which markets products under the Travel Smart brand.
Of those, he said, the top sellers are a garment steamer, an electrical outlet voltage converter and a travel iron.

On another travel front, Southwest Airlines ran up the best on-time performance for the month of August, arriving on time nearly 86 percent of the time, according to government statistics published recently in Travel Weekly magazine.
The average among the airlines in the report was 74 percent.
After Southwest the other carriers in order were Northwest, USAir, United, Continental, Delta, America West, TWA, American and Alaska.
